extraction_text: Duryodhana's ten heroic sons, led by Dushasana, were killed by Bhima after Dushasana's death.
Karna witnessed Bhima's rampage and the army's panic, then entered the battle.
King Shalya advised Karna to focus on fighting Arjuna instead of grieving.
Karna's son Vrishasena charged at Bhima in anger.
Nakula intercepted Vrishasena, destroying his banner and bow with arrows.
Vrishasena retrieved another bow and attacked Nakula with powerful weapons to avenge Dushasana's death.
Nakula became furious and shot many arrows at Vrishasena, hitting him.
Vrishasena, skilled in weapons, also struck Nakula with many divine weapons.
Vrishasena killed all of Nakula's excellent white horses from the Linshou region.
Nakula jumped from his fallen chariot, grabbed a shield and sword, and leaped like a bird.
Nakula moved through the air, killing many warriors, horses, and elephants with his sword.
Nakula alone killed two thousand well-trained warriors from various countries.
Kaurava army surrounded Nakula and shot many arrows at him, and Nakula shot back at Vrishasena.
Vrishasena, wounded and angry, shot eighteen arrows at Nakula.
Nakula continued to kill many excellent men, horses, elephants, and chariots alone.
Nakula charged at Vrishasena in battle, determined to kill him.
Vrishasena destroyed Nakula's thousand-star shield with many arrows.
Nakula wielded his fearsome iron sword.
Vrishasena broke Nakula's sword with six sharp arrows and shot many more arrows into Nakula's chest.
Nakula, with horses killed and tormented by Vrishasena, jumped onto Bhima's chariot under Arjuna's watch.
Upon learning Nakula was defeated, eleven heroes including the five sons of Drupada, Satyaki, and the five sons of Draupadi attacked the Kaurava army.
Kaurava heroes including Kritavarma, Drona, Ashvatthaman, Duryodhana, Shakuni, and others advanced against the eleven heroes.
Kaurava heroes shot countless powerful arrows at the eleven heroes, blocking their path.
Many Kuninda warriors riding elephants charged at the Kuru heroes.
The Kuninda prince fiercely shot ten large iron arrows at Kripa and his charioteer and horses.
Kripa shot the Kuninda prince with sharp arrows, causing him and his elephant to fall dead.
The younger brother of the Kuninda prince roared and threw many sun-bright iron spears at Shakuni's chariot.
Shakuni cut off the head of the still-shouting younger Kuninda prince.
A terrible battle erupted between the Kurus, Pandavas, and Srinjayas with various weapons flying and many casualties.
Shikhandi struck the enemy's elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry groups.
King Shalya rushed forward and killed many horses and weaponless elephants.
Ashvatthama's sharp arrows struck three well-equipped elephants with warriors and banners, causing them to fall like thunder-struck mountains.
The second younger brother of the Kuninda king shot excellent arrows hitting Duryodhana's chest.
Duryodhana shot many arrows piercing his opponent and the elephant's body.
The elephant king fell with the prince, bleeding profusely.
Another Kuninda prince mounted another elephant and attacked Suta and his charioteer, horses, and chariot.
Karna's arrows struck that elephant causing it to fall with its master like a thunder-struck mountain.
The elephant-riding mountain prince shot an arrow shower at the invincible chariot warrior King Karna.
The prince's arrow shower knocked down Karna with his horses, charioteer, and bow like a tree broken by wind.
Vrika fiercely shot twelve arrows deeply into the snow-mountain prince riding the elephant.
The prince's mount rushed at Vrika and crushed him with horses and chariot under its four feet.
The elephant king was struck by many fierce arrows from Nakula's son and fell with its mahout.
Yudhanyu was struck down by Prativindhya.
Another Kuninda prince riding an elephant with plow-like tusks rushed fiercely at Shakuni intending to kill him.
Shakuni beheaded the Kuninda prince.
Vrishasena (Karna's son) attacked the Pandava army, killing many soldiers, elephants, horses, and chariots.
A Kuntibhoja prince attacked Nakula's son (Shatanika) but was killed by Shatanika with a razor-headed arrow.
Vrishasena shot arrows at multiple Pandava heroes: three at Satyaki, three at Arjuna, three at Bhima, seven at Nakula, and twelve at Krishna.
Kauravas praised Vrishasena's achievements, while those who knew Arjuna's power considered Vrishasena doomed.
Arjuna saw Nakula had lost his horses and charged toward Vrishasena, who was positioned in front of Karna.

attributes.relationships: Arjuna protecting Nakula, targeting Karna's son

extraction_text: Arjuna and Vrishasena engaged in a fierce duel, compared to the ancient battle between Namuci and Indra.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Comparison to divine battle (Namuci vs Indra)

extraction_text: Vrishasena shot one hundred marvelous arrows at Arjuna and let out a roar like Namuci's when he struck Indra.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Comparison to Namuci's attack on Indra

extraction_text: Vrishasena shot multiple terrible arrows at Arjuna (hitting his armpit) and Krishna, then ten more sharp arrows at Arjuna.

attributes.relationships: Vrishasena targeting both Arjuna and Krishna

extraction_text: Arjuna became furious and shot arrows to kill Vrishasena.
Arjuna shot ten arrows hitting Vrishasena's vital points, then four razor-headed arrows that cut Vrishasena's bow, arms, and head.
Vrishasena fell dead from his chariot, compared to a flowering sal tree broken by wind.
Karna saw his son fall and, filled with grief, immediately drove his chariot toward Arjuna.
Karna witnessed Vrishasena's death and shed tears of sorrow.
Karna became furious, his eyes turning copper-red, and charged toward Arjuna to challenge him.

attributes.relationships: Longstanding rivalry between Karna and Arjuna

extraction_text: The two chariots covered with tiger skins and bright as suns met on the battlefield like two suns encountering each other.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Celestial comparison of chariots to suns

extraction_text: Karna and Arjuna prepare for a one-on-one duel in the Kurukshetra War.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Compared to divine beings like Indra and Vritra, described with celestial imagery.

extraction_text: The armies and kings witness the two heroes with their chariots, banners, and weapons, expressing awe and admiration.

attributes.relationships: Karna is supported by the Kaurava army; Arjuna is supported by the Pandava army.

extraction_text: The Kaurava army surrounds Karna to encourage him, while the Pandava army surrounds Arjuna.

attributes.relationships: Karna is allied with Duryodhana and the Kauravas; Arjuna is allied with the Pandavas, led by Dhrishtadyumna.

extraction_text: Karna and Arjuna are described as sons of gods (Surya and Indra respectively), equipped for battle and compared to legendary warriors.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Divine parentage and comparisons to gods and epic heroes like Rama and Vishnu.

extraction_text: The two warriors are metaphorically described as dice in the gambling of war, representing their sides in the conflict.

attributes.relationships: Karna represents the Kaurava side; Arjuna represents the Pandava side in the Kurukshetra War.

extraction_text: The armies of both sides stand arrayed for battle, with Karna and Arjuna preparing to duel.
A great debate arises among all beings in the sky about who will win between Karna and Arjuna.
Various cosmic entities take sides: Devas, Danavas, Gandharvas, Pisachas, Nagas, and Rakshasas are divided in their support.
The sky and stars worry for Karna, while the earth worries for Arjuna like a mother for her son.
Rivers, oceans, mountains, forests, herbs, jewels, treasures, Vedas, Puranas, Upanishads, and serpents support Arjuna.

supernatural_elements: Natural elements and knowledge systems taking sides

extraction_text: Asuras, Yakshas, Kinnaras, celestial beings, and birds support Karna.

supernatural_elements: Demonic and celestial beings choosing sides

extraction_text: Wolves, carnivores, auspicious animals, and birds anticipate Arjuna's victory.
Major deities including Vasus, Maruts, Rudras, Vishvedevas, Ashvins, Agni, Indra, Soma, Vayu, and the ten directional guardians support Arjuna, while Adityas support Karna.
Devas, ancestors, Yama, Kubera, Varuna, sages, and Gandharvas led by Tumburu are Arjuna's supporters.
Numerous celestial beings, sages, and ancestors travel to the battlefield to witness the duel between Karna and Arjuna.
Brahma arrives with sages, Prajapatis, and Shiva in a celestial chariot.
The Devas ask Brahma to grant victory to both Karna and Arjuna equally.
Indra (Sakra) respectfully addressed Brahma, expressing concern that the deaths of Karna and Arjuna would lead to the destruction of the world.
Indra requested Brahma to declare that both Karna and Arjuna should be victorious.
Brahma and Shiva (Ishana) responded to Indra, stating that Arjuna (Vijaya) must be victorious.

attributes.reason: Arjuna's superior qualities and divine nature

extraction_text: Brahma and Shiva explained that Arjuna and Krishna are the ancient sages Nara and Narayana, creators and rulers of all existence.

Brahma and Shiva decreed that Karna should go to the best abode in the three worlds (heaven of the Vasus or Maruts) and be honored there with Drona and Bhishma, while the two dark princes (Krishna and Arjuna) should win.

attributes.decree: Karna's heavenly fate, Krishna and Arjuna's victory

extraction_text: Indra gathered all beings and announced that Brahma and Shiva's words were final for the benefit of the universe.
All beings expressed amazement and praised Krishna and Arjuna upon hearing Indra's announcement.
The gods showered fragrant, colorful flowers from the sky, and celestial music filled heaven and earth.
All gods, Danavas, and Gandharvas gathered to witness the unparalleled single combat between the two lion-like heroes (Karna and Arjuna).
Many great heroes assembled around Krishna, Arjuna, Karna, and King Shalya, blowing their conches.
The terrifying battle began between the two heroes, likened to Indra fighting Shambara.
The two heroes attacked each other fiercely from their brightly decorated chariots.
Karna's banner featured a jeweled, snake-like elephant goad resembling Indra's bow, while Arjuna's banner featured a fierce, sun-like ape leader.
The ape on Arjuna's banner, eager for battle, roared and leaped onto Karna's banner to challenge it.
The monkey-bannered hero (Hanuman on Arjuna's banner) and the elephant rope (Karna's banner) engage in a symbolic battle.
Krishna and Shalya engage in a battle of fierce glances.
Arjuna and Karna engage in a battle of fierce glances.
Karna asks Shalya what he will do if Arjuna kills Karna in battle.
Shalya vows to kill both Krishna and Arjuna alone if Karna is slain.
Arjuna asks Krishna the same question.
Krishna assures Arjuna that Karna cannot kill him, vowing to kill Karna and Shalya himself if it were to happen.
Arjuna confidently declares he will destroy Karna and all his possessions in battle to avenge Draupadi's insult.
